chapter_text:
CHAPTER 7 — CHEMICAL BONDING

Introduction

In earlier chapters we learnt that matter is made of atoms, and that each atom has a tiny nucleus surrounded by electrons arranged in shells. In nature, however, free single atoms are rare — except for the noble gases. Most atoms are found joined together with other atoms, forming molecules or large ionic crystals. The force of attraction that holds atoms together in a molecule or a compound is called a CHEMICAL BOND, and the process by which atoms combine is called CHEMICAL BONDING. This chapter explains WHY atoms combine and the main WAYS in which they do so — ionic (electrovalent) bonding, covalent bonding and the coordinate (dative) bond.

7.1 WHY DO ATOMS COMBINE? THE OCTET RULE

The key to bonding lies in the electronic configuration of the atom. The noble gases — helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon — are chemically unreactive (inert). Their outermost shells are completely filled: helium has 2 electrons in its only shell, and the others have 8 electrons in their outermost shell (an OCTET). A completely filled outermost shell is the most STABLE arrangement of electrons.

All other atoms have incomplete outer shells and are therefore comparatively unstable and reactive. When such atoms react, they tend to gain, lose or share electrons so as to achieve a stable noble-gas configuration — that is, 8 electrons (or 2, for the smallest atoms) in their outermost shell. This tendency is summarised in the OCTET RULE: atoms combine in such a way that each attains eight electrons in its valence (outermost) shell, like the nearest noble gas. The smallest atoms (H, Li, Be) aim instead for the helium configuration of 2 electrons — sometimes called the DUET rule.

The electrons in the outermost shell are the VALENCE ELECTRONS; they alone take part in bonding. The combining capacity of an atom — its VALENCY — depends on how many electrons it must gain, lose or share to complete its octet. This is the ELECTRONIC THEORY OF VALENCY, proposed by Kossel and Lewis (1916). According to it, there are two principal ways to attain a noble-gas configuration:
  (1) by TRANSFER of electrons from one atom to another → IONIC (electrovalent) bond;
  (2) by SHARING of electrons between atoms → COVALENT bond.

7.2 IONIC (ELECTROVALENT) BONDING

An IONIC BOND (also called an electrovalent bond) is formed by the COMPLETE TRANSFER of one or more electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom. The atom that loses electrons becomes a positively charged ion (a CATION); the atom that gains them becomes a negatively charged ion (an ANION). The oppositely charged ions are then held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction — this force IS the ionic bond.

(a) Formation of sodium chloride (NaCl).
Sodium (Z = 11) has the configuration 2, 8, 1 — one electron more than the stable neon arrangement. Chlorine (Z = 17) has 2, 8, 7 — one electron short of the stable argon arrangement. When they react, sodium DONATES its single valence electron to chlorine:
  Na (2, 8, 1) → Na⁺ (2, 8) + e⁻
  Cl (2, 8, 7) + e⁻ → Cl⁻ (2, 8, 8)
The sodium ion Na⁺ now has a neon configuration; the chloride ion Cl⁻ has an argon configuration. Both are stable. The Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions attract each other and pack together in a regular three-dimensional lattice, forming the ionic compound sodium chloride.

(b) Formation of magnesium chloride (MgCl₂).
Magnesium (Z = 12) has the configuration 2, 8, 2 — two valence electrons to lose. Each chlorine atom can accept only ONE electron. So one magnesium atom transfers its two electrons to TWO chlorine atoms:
  Mg (2, 8, 2) → Mg²⁺ (2, 8) + 2e⁻
  2 Cl (2, 8, 7) + 2e⁻ → 2 Cl⁻ (2, 8, 8)
The formula is therefore MgCl₂ — one Mg²⁺ ion for every two Cl⁻ ions, keeping the compound electrically neutral.

(c) Formation of calcium oxide (CaO).
Calcium (Z = 20) has the configuration 2, 8, 8, 2 — two valence electrons to lose. Oxygen (Z = 8) has 2, 6 — it needs two electrons to complete its octet. Here the transfer is one-to-one:
  Ca (2, 8, 8, 2) → Ca²⁺ (2, 8, 8) + 2e⁻
  O (2, 6) + 2e⁻ → O²⁻ (2, 8)
The Ca²⁺ and O²⁻ ions combine in a 1 : 1 ratio, giving calcium oxide CaO.

Properties of ionic compounds.
Because ionic compounds are held together by strong electrostatic forces extending throughout a giant crystal lattice, they have characteristic properties:
  • They are CRYSTALLINE SOLIDS at room temperature, with the ions arranged in a regular geometric pattern.
  • They have HIGH MELTING POINTS and HIGH BOILING POINTS, because a large amount of energy is needed to overcome the strong ionic attractions throughout the lattice.
  • They are generally SOLUBLE IN WATER (and in other polar solvents) but insoluble in non-polar organic solvents like petrol or kerosene.
  • In the SOLID state they do NOT conduct electricity, because the ions are locked in fixed positions. But when MOLTEN (melted) or DISSOLVED in water, the ions become free to move, so molten and aqueous ionic compounds CONDUCT electricity. They are electrolytes.
  • They are usually hard but brittle.

7.3 COVALENT BONDING

When two atoms — usually both non-metals — combine, neither has a strong tendency to give up electrons completely. Instead they achieve stable octets by SHARING electrons. A COVALENT BOND is the bond formed by the MUTUAL SHARING of one or more pairs of electrons between two atoms. Each shared pair counts towards the octet of BOTH atoms. A shared pair is often shown as a line (—) between the atom symbols; the arrangement showing all valence electrons as dots is called a LEWIS (electron-dot) structure.

Single, double and triple bonds.
  • A SINGLE bond is the sharing of ONE pair of electrons (one shared pair), e.g. H—H in hydrogen, Cl—Cl in chlorine.
  • A DOUBLE bond is the sharing of TWO pairs of electrons, e.g. O=O in oxygen, and each C=O in carbon dioxide.
  • A TRIPLE bond is the sharing of THREE pairs of electrons, e.g. N≡N in nitrogen.

Examples.
  • Hydrogen molecule (H₂): each H atom has 1 electron and needs 1 more to reach the helium duet. The two atoms share one pair → a single bond, H—H.
  • Chlorine molecule (Cl₂): each Cl (2, 8, 7) needs one more electron. They share one pair → Cl—Cl. Each Cl also keeps three non-bonding 'lone pairs'.
  • Oxygen molecule (O₂): each O (2, 6) needs two electrons; the atoms share two pairs → a double bond, O=O.
  • Nitrogen molecule (N₂): each N (2, 5) needs three electrons; they share three pairs → a triple bond, N≡N. This triple bond is very strong, which makes N₂ rather unreactive.
  • Water (H₂O): the oxygen atom shares one electron pair with each of two hydrogen atoms (two single O—H bonds). Oxygen thus completes its octet, and each hydrogen completes its duet.
  • Methane (CH₄): carbon (2, 4) shares one electron pair with each of four hydrogen atoms, forming four C—H single bonds; carbon attains an octet and each hydrogen a duet.
  • Carbon dioxide (CO₂): carbon forms a double bond with each of two oxygen atoms, O=C=O; all three atoms complete their octets.
  • Ammonia (NH₃): nitrogen (2, 5) shares one electron pair with each of three hydrogen atoms (three N—H single bonds) and is left with one lone pair; nitrogen completes its octet and each hydrogen its duet.

Properties of covalent compounds.
Covalent compounds usually exist as discrete molecules with only weak forces BETWEEN the molecules, so:
  • They are usually gases, liquids or soft solids with LOW MELTING POINTS and LOW BOILING POINTS.
  • They are generally POOR CONDUCTORS of electricity (non-electrolytes), because they contain no free ions or free electrons.
  • They are often INSOLUBLE IN WATER but soluble in organic (non-polar) solvents — though some polar covalent compounds (like sugar, alcohol) do dissolve in water.
  • Their reactions are usually slower than those of ionic compounds.

7.4 POLAR AND NON-POLAR COVALENT BONDS

When the two atoms sharing a bond are IDENTICAL (as in H₂, O₂, N₂, Cl₂), the shared electron pair is pulled equally by both nuclei. The bond is then a NON-POLAR covalent bond and the molecule has no separation of charge.

When the two atoms are DIFFERENT, one atom usually attracts the shared electrons more strongly than the other (it is more electronegative). The shared pair lies closer to that atom, giving it a small negative charge (δ−) and leaving the other atom slightly positive (δ+). Such a bond is a POLAR covalent bond. For example, in the H—Cl bond, chlorine is more electronegative, so it is δ− and hydrogen is δ+. Water (H₂O) is a polar molecule for the same reason — oxygen pulls the shared electrons towards itself, making the molecule a tiny dipole. Polarity explains why polar substances dissolve readily in polar solvents such as water.

7.5 THE COORDINATE (DATIVE) BOND

In an ordinary covalent bond, EACH atom contributes one electron to the shared pair. In a COORDINATE BOND (also called a dative bond), the shared pair of electrons is provided ENTIRELY by ONE of the two atoms; the other atom contributes none but shares the pair. The atom that donates the pair is the DONOR; the atom that accepts a share is the ACCEPTOR. Once formed, a coordinate bond is identical to a normal covalent bond. It is shown by an arrow (→) pointing from donor to acceptor.

Examples.
  • Ammonium ion (NH₄⁺): the nitrogen atom in ammonia (NH₃) has a lone pair of electrons. When ammonia meets a hydrogen ion H⁺ (which has no electrons), the nitrogen donates its lone pair to form a new N→H bond. The result is the ammonium ion NH₄⁺, in which all four N—H bonds are equivalent.
  • Hydronium ion (H₃O⁺): the oxygen atom in water has lone pairs. When water accepts an H⁺ ion, oxygen donates a lone pair to form an O→H coordinate bond, giving the hydronium ion H₃O⁺ — this is what an acid actually forms in water.

7.6 COMPARISON OF IONIC AND COVALENT BONDS

Briefly contrasting the two main bond types:
  • FORMATION — ionic: complete transfer of electrons (metal → non-metal); covalent: sharing of electrons (usually non-metal + non-metal).
  • PARTICLES — ionic compounds are made of ions in a giant lattice; covalent compounds are made of discrete molecules.
  • MELTING/BOILING POINTS — high for ionic, low for covalent.
  • ELECTRICAL CONDUCTIVITY — ionic compounds conduct when molten or in solution; covalent compounds generally do not conduct.
  • SOLUBILITY — ionic compounds dissolve in water (polar solvents); covalent compounds usually dissolve in non-polar (organic) solvents.
  • STATE — ionic compounds are crystalline solids; covalent compounds are often gases, liquids or soft solids.

SUMMARY

- Atoms combine to attain the stable, fully-filled outermost-shell (noble-gas) configuration — the octet rule (or duet for the smallest atoms).
- Valence electrons take part in bonding; valency is the number of electrons gained, lost or shared.
- An IONIC (electrovalent) bond forms by complete electron transfer from a metal to a non-metal, producing oppositely charged ions held by electrostatic attraction (NaCl, MgCl₂, CaO).
- Ionic compounds are crystalline solids with high melting/boiling points, soluble in water, and conduct electricity when molten or dissolved.
- A COVALENT bond forms by the sharing of one (single), two (double) or three (triple) electron pairs between atoms (H₂, O₂, N₂, Cl₂, H₂O, CH₄, CO₂, NH₃).
- Covalent compounds have low melting/boiling points, are poor conductors, and are often insoluble in water.
- Bonds between identical atoms are non-polar; bonds between different atoms are usually polar (δ+ and δ−).
- A COORDINATE (dative) bond is a covalent bond in which the shared pair comes entirely from one atom (NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺).

worksheet.title: Worksheet — Chemical Bonding (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Secondary Science & Technology (212) official Worksheet-7 for Lesson 7. Attempt all questions. Refer to the periodic table for atomic numbers and electronic configurations where needed.

questions.question: Why do atoms combine to form molecules or compounds? Answer in terms of the octet rule.
questions.answer:
Atoms combine to attain a STABLE electronic configuration. The noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, ...) are unreactive because their outermost shells are completely filled — 2 electrons for helium and 8 (an octet) for the others. A full outer shell is the most stable arrangement.

All other atoms have incomplete outer shells and are therefore relatively unstable and reactive. When they react, they gain, lose or share valence electrons so as to reach the nearest noble-gas configuration. This tendency is the OCTET RULE: atoms combine so that each attains eight electrons in its valence shell (or two, for the smallest atoms — the duet). Forming a chemical bond lowers the energy and gives each atom a stable octet, which is why bonding occurs.
questions.explanation: Stability of noble-gas configuration drives bonding; state the octet rule.

questions.question: Explain the formation of sodium chloride (NaCl) by the transfer of electrons. Show the electronic configurations.
questions.answer:
Sodium chloride is an IONIC compound formed by complete electron transfer from sodium (a metal) to chlorine (a non-metal).

Sodium (Z = 11): configuration 2, 8, 1 — one electron more than neon. It readily LOSES this single valence electron:
  Na (2, 8, 1) → Na⁺ (2, 8) + e⁻
Chlorine (Z = 17): configuration 2, 8, 7 — one electron short of argon. It GAINS one electron:
  Cl (2, 8, 7) + e⁻ → Cl⁻ (2, 8, 8)

The sodium ion now has a neon configuration and the chloride ion an argon configuration — both stable octets. The oppositely charged Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions attract one another by strong electrostatic forces and arrange themselves in a regular crystal lattice, forming solid NaCl in a 1 : 1 ratio.
questions.explanation: One-electron transfer Na → Cl; both reach octet; ions held electrostatically.

questions.question: Explain why one magnesium atom combines with two chlorine atoms to form MgCl2.
questions.answer:
Magnesium (Z = 12) has the configuration 2, 8, 2 — it has TWO valence electrons to lose to reach the neon configuration. Chlorine (Z = 17) has 2, 8, 7 — each chlorine atom can accept only ONE electron to complete its octet.

Since magnesium must lose two electrons but each chlorine can take only one, ONE magnesium atom transfers its two electrons to TWO chlorine atoms:
  Mg (2, 8, 2) → Mg²⁺ (2, 8) + 2e⁻
  2 Cl (2, 8, 7) + 2e⁻ → 2 Cl⁻ (2, 8, 8)

This gives one Mg²⁺ ion and two Cl⁻ ions, so the compound is MgCl₂. The 1 : 2 ratio is required to balance the charges and keep the compound electrically neutral.
questions.explanation: Mg loses 2 e⁻; each Cl gains 1 e⁻; charge balance gives the 1:2 ratio.

questions.question: List four characteristic properties of ionic compounds.
questions.answer:
Ionic compounds, held together by strong electrostatic forces in a giant lattice, show these properties:
  1. They are hard, brittle CRYSTALLINE SOLIDS at room temperature, with ions in a regular pattern.
  2. They have HIGH melting points and HIGH boiling points, because a lot of energy is needed to overcome the strong ionic attractions throughout the lattice.
  3. They are generally SOLUBLE IN WATER (and other polar solvents) but insoluble in non-polar organic solvents.
  4. They do NOT conduct electricity in the solid state (ions are fixed), but they DO conduct when molten or dissolved in water, because the ions are then free to move.
questions.explanation: Crystalline solid, high m.p./b.p., water-soluble, conduct when molten/aqueous.

questions.question: What is a covalent bond? Explain the formation of the chlorine molecule (Cl2).
questions.answer:
A COVALENT BOND is the bond formed by the mutual SHARING of one or more pairs of electrons between two atoms, so that each atom attains a stable octet (or duet).

Chlorine atom (Z = 17) has the configuration 2, 8, 7 — it is one electron short of the argon octet. Neither chlorine atom will give up an electron completely (both are identical non-metals), so two chlorine atoms instead SHARE one pair of electrons: each atom contributes one electron to the shared pair.

The shared pair is counted in the outer shell of BOTH atoms, so each chlorine now effectively has 8 outer electrons. This single shared pair is a SINGLE covalent bond, written Cl—Cl. Each chlorine atom also keeps three non-bonding lone pairs.
questions.explanation: Define covalent bond; Cl2 shares one pair → single bond, both reach octet.

questions.question: Distinguish between a single, a double and a triple covalent bond, giving one example of each.
questions.answer:
The type of covalent bond depends on the number of electron PAIRS shared between two atoms:
  • SINGLE bond — one pair of electrons is shared (one shared pair). Example: hydrogen H—H, or chlorine Cl—Cl.
  • DOUBLE bond — two pairs of electrons are shared. Example: oxygen O=O, and each bond in carbon dioxide O=C=O.
  • TRIPLE bond — three pairs of electrons are shared. Example: nitrogen N≡N.

The more pairs shared, the stronger and shorter the bond. The triple bond in N₂ is very strong, which is why nitrogen gas is rather unreactive.
questions.explanation: 1 pair = single (H2); 2 pairs = double (O2); 3 pairs = triple (N2).

questions.question: Distinguish between a polar and a non-polar covalent bond with one example of each.
questions.answer:
Both are covalent bonds (formed by sharing electrons), but they differ in how equally the shared pair is shared:

NON-POLAR covalent bond: formed between two IDENTICAL atoms. The shared electron pair is attracted equally by both nuclei, so there is no separation of charge. Examples: H₂ (H—H), O₂, N₂, Cl₂.

POLAR covalent bond: formed between two DIFFERENT atoms. One atom (the more electronegative) attracts the shared pair more strongly, so the electrons lie closer to it. That atom gets a small negative charge (δ−) and the other a small positive charge (δ+). Example: the H—Cl bond, where chlorine is δ− and hydrogen δ+; water (H₂O) is similarly polar.
questions.explanation: Non-polar = identical atoms, equal sharing; polar = different atoms, δ+/δ−.

questions.question: What is a coordinate (dative) bond? Explain the formation of the ammonium ion (NH4+).
questions.answer:
A COORDINATE (or dative) bond is a covalent bond in which the shared pair of electrons is supplied ENTIRELY by ONE of the two atoms (the donor); the other atom (the acceptor) contributes no electrons but shares the pair. Once formed, it is identical to an ordinary covalent bond. It is shown by an arrow (→) from donor to acceptor.

Formation of NH₄⁺: In an ammonia molecule (NH₃), the nitrogen atom has three N—H bonds and one LONE PAIR of electrons. A hydrogen ion (H⁺) has no electrons of its own. The nitrogen DONATES its lone pair to the H⁺ ion, forming a new N→H coordinate bond:
  NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺
In the ammonium ion all four N—H bonds become equivalent, and the ion carries a single positive charge.
questions.explanation: Coordinate bond: shared pair from one atom; N donates lone pair to H⁺ → NH4+.

questions.question: Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water, but not in the solid state?
questions.answer:
Electrical conduction requires charged particles that are FREE to move. In an ionic compound the charge carriers are the ions (cations and anions).

In the SOLID state, the ions are locked in fixed positions in the crystal lattice by strong electrostatic forces; they can only vibrate, not move from place to place. With no mobile charge carriers, the solid does NOT conduct electricity.

When the compound is MELTED (molten) or DISSOLVED in water, the lattice breaks up and the ions become free to move about. When a voltage is applied, the positive ions move to the cathode and the negative ions to the anode, carrying the current. Hence molten and aqueous ionic compounds conduct electricity (they are electrolytes).
questions.explanation: Conduction needs free-moving ions; solid lattice is fixed, molten/aqueous is mobile.

questions.question: Compare ionic and covalent compounds with respect to (a) the way the bond is formed, (b) the particles present, (c) melting and boiling points, (d) electrical conductivity, and (e) solubility.
questions.answer:
(a) FORMATION — Ionic: by complete TRANSFER of electrons from a metal to a non-metal. Covalent: by SHARING of electron pairs, usually between two non-metals.

(b) PARTICLES — Ionic compounds are made of oppositely charged IONS arranged in a giant three-dimensional lattice. Covalent compounds are made of discrete MOLECULES.

(c) MELTING / BOILING POINTS — Ionic: HIGH, because strong electrostatic forces extend throughout the whole lattice and a lot of energy is needed to break them. Covalent: LOW, because the forces BETWEEN molecules are weak.

(d) ELECTRICAL CONDUCTIVITY — Ionic compounds do not conduct as solids but DO conduct when molten or dissolved (free ions). Covalent compounds generally do NOT conduct, because they have no free ions or electrons.

(e) SOLUBILITY — Ionic compounds are generally soluble in water and other polar solvents, insoluble in non-polar solvents. Covalent compounds are usually insoluble in water but soluble in non-polar (organic) solvents (though some polar covalent compounds dissolve in water).
questions.explanation: Five-point comparison: transfer vs sharing; ions vs molecules; high vs low m.p./b.p.; conduct when molten/aqueous vs non-conducting; water-soluble vs organic-soluble.

questions.question: State the octet rule and give one reason why atoms try to obey it.
questions.answer:
The OCTET RULE states that atoms combine (by gaining, losing or sharing electrons) so as to attain eight electrons in their outermost (valence) shell, like the nearest noble gas. (The smallest atoms aim for a duet of 2.)

Reason: a completely filled outer shell — as in the noble gases — is the most STABLE, lowest-energy arrangement of electrons. By achieving an octet, an atom reaches this stable configuration, which is why bonding occurs.

questions.question: An element has the electronic configuration 2, 8, 7. State its valency and whether it will lose, gain or share electrons.
questions.answer:
The outermost shell has 7 valence electrons, which is more than 4. To complete its octet it needs just ONE more electron, so it tends to GAIN one electron (or share one pair).

Valency = 8 − 7 = 1. This element behaves like a halogen (e.g. chlorine, configuration 2, 8, 7), forming an ion with a 1− charge or one single covalent bond.

questions.question: Explain the formation of calcium oxide (CaO) by electron transfer, showing the configurations of the ions formed.
questions.answer:
Calcium oxide is an ionic compound formed by transfer of electrons from calcium (metal) to oxygen (non-metal).

Calcium (Z = 20): configuration 2, 8, 8, 2 — it has two valence electrons to lose.
Oxygen (Z = 8): configuration 2, 6 — it needs two electrons to complete its octet.

Calcium transfers BOTH its valence electrons to one oxygen atom (a one-to-one transfer):
  Ca (2, 8, 8, 2) → Ca²⁺ (2, 8, 8) + 2e⁻
  O (2, 6) + 2e⁻ → O²⁻ (2, 8)

The Ca²⁺ ion has an argon configuration and the O²⁻ ion a neon configuration — both stable. The 2+ and 2− ions attract each other strongly and combine in a 1 : 1 ratio, giving CaO.

questions.question: Define the terms cation and anion, giving one example of each.
questions.answer:
CATION: a positively charged ion formed when an atom LOSES one or more electrons. Example: the sodium ion Na⁺ (formed when Na loses one electron).

ANION: a negatively charged ion formed when an atom GAINS one or more electrons. Example: the chloride ion Cl⁻ (formed when Cl gains one electron). Other examples: cation Mg²⁺, anion O²⁻.

questions.question: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points but are also brittle?
questions.answer:
In an ionic compound the oppositely charged ions are arranged in a giant three-dimensional LATTICE, held by strong electrostatic forces that extend throughout the whole crystal.

HIGH MELTING POINT: to melt the compound, these strong lattice-wide attractions must be overcome, which requires a large amount of heat energy. Hence ionic compounds melt (and boil) at high temperatures.

BRITTLENESS: when a force is applied and one layer of ions slides over another, ions of the SAME charge come to face each other. The like charges repel strongly, and the crystal splits apart along that plane. This is why ionic crystals, though hard, are brittle and shatter rather than bend.

questions.question: Why are ionic compounds generally soluble in water but insoluble in petrol?
questions.answer:
Water is a POLAR solvent: its molecules have δ+ and δ− ends. These polar water molecules surround the ions of an ionic compound, attract them, and pull them out of the lattice — so the compound dissolves in water.

Petrol (and other organic solvents) is NON-POLAR: it has no charged ends to attract the ions, so it cannot pull the ions apart. Hence ionic compounds are insoluble in petrol and similar non-polar solvents. (Rule of thumb: like dissolves like — polar dissolves ionic/polar.)

questions.question: Describe the bonding in a water molecule (H2O) and explain how each atom attains a stable configuration.
questions.answer:
In water, the central oxygen atom (Z = 8, configuration 2, 6) needs 2 more electrons to complete its octet. Each hydrogen atom (1 electron) needs 1 more to reach the helium duet.

Oxygen SHARES one electron pair with each of the two hydrogen atoms, forming two single O—H covalent bonds. Each shared pair contains one electron from oxygen and one from hydrogen.

Result: oxygen now has 8 electrons in its outer shell (its two original lone pairs plus the two shared pairs) — a complete octet. Each hydrogen now effectively has 2 electrons — a complete duet. Oxygen also keeps two lone pairs, which is why the water molecule is bent and polar.

questions.question: What is a Lewis structure? What does a lone pair represent in it?
questions.answer:
A LEWIS STRUCTURE (or electron-dot structure) is a diagram that shows all the VALENCE electrons of the atoms in a molecule, using dots (and lines or shared dots for bonds). It shows which electrons are shared between atoms (bonding pairs) and which are not.

A LONE PAIR is a pair of valence electrons on an atom that is NOT involved in bonding — it belongs to that atom alone. For example, in ammonia (NH₃) nitrogen has one lone pair, and in water oxygen has two lone pairs.

questions.question: Explain the bonding in carbon dioxide (CO2). What types of bonds are present?
questions.answer:
Carbon (Z = 6, configuration 2, 4) has 4 valence electrons and needs 4 more for an octet. Each oxygen (2, 6) needs 2 more electrons.

Carbon forms a DOUBLE bond with EACH of the two oxygen atoms, sharing two electron pairs with each. The structure is O=C=O.

By sharing two pairs with each oxygen, carbon shares a total of 8 electrons (4 pairs), completing its octet. Each oxygen, by sharing two pairs with carbon, also completes its octet. So CO₂ contains TWO double covalent bonds and no single, triple, ionic or coordinate bonds.

questions.question: Compare the bonding in O2 and N2. Why is N2 less reactive than O2?
questions.answer:
O₂: each oxygen atom (2, 6) needs 2 electrons, so the two atoms share TWO pairs → a DOUBLE bond, O=O.

N₂: each nitrogen atom (2, 5) needs 3 electrons, so the two atoms share THREE pairs → a TRIPLE bond, N≡N.

A triple bond is stronger and shorter than a double bond because more shared pairs hold the nuclei together more tightly. Breaking the very strong N≡N triple bond requires a large amount of energy, so N₂ is rather unreactive (inert) under ordinary conditions. The weaker O=O double bond is easier to break, so O₂ is more reactive and readily takes part in reactions such as combustion and rusting.

questions.question: State two differences between ionic and covalent compounds in terms of physical properties.
questions.answer:
1. MELTING / BOILING POINTS: ionic compounds have HIGH melting and boiling points (strong lattice-wide forces); covalent compounds have LOW melting and boiling points (weak forces between molecules).

2. ELECTRICAL CONDUCTIVITY: ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water (free ions); covalent compounds generally do NOT conduct (no free ions or electrons).

(Other valid differences: ionic compounds dissolve in water, covalent ones usually in organic solvents; ionic = crystalline solids, covalent often = gases/liquids/soft solids.)

questions.question: Why is HCl a polar molecule while Cl2 is non-polar?
questions.answer:
In Cl₂, the two atoms sharing the bond are IDENTICAL chlorine atoms. They attract the shared electron pair equally, so there is no separation of charge — the bond and the molecule are NON-POLAR.

In HCl, the two atoms are DIFFERENT. Chlorine is more electronegative than hydrogen, so it pulls the shared electron pair closer to itself. Chlorine therefore becomes slightly negative (δ−) and hydrogen slightly positive (δ+). This separation of charge makes the H—Cl bond — and the HCl molecule — POLAR.

questions.question: List two properties of covalent compounds.
questions.answer:
Two properties of covalent compounds:
1. They have LOW melting and boiling points, because the forces between their molecules are weak (many are gases or liquids at room temperature).
2. They are generally POOR conductors of electricity (non-electrolytes), because they contain no free ions or electrons.

(Another valid property: they are usually insoluble in water but soluble in non-polar organic solvents.)

questions.question: Explain the formation of the hydronium ion (H3O+) as a coordinate bond.
questions.answer:
A coordinate (dative) bond is a covalent bond in which the shared pair of electrons comes entirely from ONE atom.

In a water molecule (H₂O), the oxygen atom has two LONE PAIRS of electrons. A hydrogen ion (H⁺) has no electrons of its own and needs a share of a pair to become stable.

The oxygen atom DONATES one of its lone pairs to the H⁺ ion, forming a new O→H coordinate bond:
  H₂O + H⁺ → H₃O⁺

The resulting hydronium ion H₃O⁺ has three O—H bonds (all equivalent once formed) and carries a single positive charge. This is the ion that an acid actually produces when dissolved in water.

questions.question: How does a coordinate bond differ from an ordinary covalent bond?
questions.answer:
In an ORDINARY covalent bond, EACH of the two atoms contributes one electron to the shared pair (one each).

In a COORDINATE (dative) bond, the whole shared pair is supplied by just ONE atom (the donor); the other atom (the acceptor) contributes no electrons but shares the pair.

The difference is only in the ORIGIN of the shared electrons. Once formed, a coordinate bond is identical in strength and behaviour to a normal covalent bond. It is shown by an arrow (→) from donor to acceptor instead of a plain line.

questions.question: A student is given two white solids, X and Y. X melts at a high temperature, dissolves in water and conducts electricity in solution. Y melts at a low temperature, does not dissolve in water and does not conduct. Classify X and Y and justify.
questions.answer:
X is an IONIC compound. Evidence: a high melting point (strong electrostatic forces in a giant lattice), solubility in water (a polar solvent surrounds and frees the ions), and electrical conductivity in solution (free-moving ions carry the current). These are the signature properties of an ionic compound (e.g. common salt, NaCl).

Y is a COVALENT compound. Evidence: a low melting point (weak forces between discrete molecules), insolubility in water (it is likely non-polar, so polar water cannot dissolve it), and no electrical conductivity (no free ions or electrons). These are typical of a covalent compound (e.g. wax, naphthalene).

questions.question: State two ways in which an ionic bond differs from a covalent bond in the way it is formed.
questions.answer:
1. WAY OF FORMATION: an ionic bond forms by the complete TRANSFER of electrons from one atom to another, whereas a covalent bond forms by the SHARING of electron pairs between atoms.

2. ATOMS INVOLVED: an ionic bond usually forms between a METAL (which loses electrons) and a NON-METAL (which gains them), whereas a covalent bond usually forms between two NON-METALS. (As a result, ionic bonding produces ions, while covalent bonding produces neutral molecules.)

questions.question: An element X has the configuration 2, 8, 3. Will it form an ionic or a covalent compound with chlorine, and what will be its valency?
questions.answer:
Element X has 3 valence electrons (configuration 2, 8, 3) — this is a metal (it resembles aluminium). Since 3 ≤ 4, it tends to LOSE its 3 valence electrons to form an X³⁺ ion. Its valency is 3.

With chlorine (a non-metal that gains electrons), X will form an IONIC compound by electron transfer. X loses 3 electrons, and three chlorine atoms each gain one, so the formula is XCl₃.

questions.question: Explain why the bond in a hydrogen molecule (H2) is a single covalent bond.
questions.answer:
A hydrogen atom has 1 electron and needs just 1 more to reach the stable helium configuration of 2 electrons (a duet). Hydrogen is a non-metal, so instead of transferring electrons, two hydrogen atoms SHARE their electrons.

Each atom contributes one electron to a single shared pair. Sharing ONE pair of electrons is, by definition, a SINGLE covalent bond, written H—H. Through this shared pair each hydrogen atom effectively has 2 electrons, completing its duet.

questions.question: Element P has configuration 2, 8, 1 and element Q has configuration 2, 8, 7. Predict the type of bond, the ions formed and the formula of the compound.
questions.answer:
Element P (2, 8, 1) is a metal with 1 valence electron; it tends to LOSE that electron to form P⁺ (configuration 2, 8). Element Q (2, 8, 7) is a non-metal with 7 valence electrons; it tends to GAIN 1 electron to form Q⁻ (configuration 2, 8, 8).

Since P loses an electron and Q gains it, an IONIC (electrovalent) bond is formed by electron transfer:
  P → P⁺ + e⁻
  Q + e⁻ → Q⁻

The P⁺ and Q⁻ ions combine in a 1 : 1 ratio (charges balance), so the formula of the compound is PQ. (This is exactly analogous to sodium and chlorine forming NaCl.)

questions.question: Why does a sodium atom react readily while a neon atom does not, even though both have a full inner shell?
questions.answer:
Neon (2, 8) has a COMPLETE outermost shell of 8 electrons — a stable octet. It has no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons, so it does not react (it is a noble gas).

Sodium (2, 8, 1) has just ONE electron in its outermost shell, so its outer shell is INCOMPLETE and unstable. By losing this single electron, sodium attains the stable neon configuration (2, 8). Because losing one electron is easy and gives a stable octet, sodium reacts readily. The difference lies in whether the OUTERMOST shell is full, not the inner shells.

questions.question: A liquid does not conduct electricity and boils at 65 °C. Another student claims it must be ionic. Evaluate this claim.
questions.answer:
The claim is INCORRECT. The two pieces of evidence both point AWAY from an ionic compound:

1. A boiling point of only 65 °C is very LOW. Ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points (often several hundred degrees) because of strong lattice forces. A low boiling point indicates weak forces between molecules — typical of a COVALENT compound.

2. The liquid does NOT conduct electricity. A molten or liquid ionic compound WOULD conduct, because it contains free-moving ions. A non-conducting liquid has no free ions, which again indicates a covalent compound.

Conclusion: both clues indicate the liquid is a COVALENT compound, not ionic. The student's claim should be rejected.

questions.question: What are valence electrons? Why are they important in chemical bonding?
questions.answer:
VALENCE ELECTRONS are the electrons present in the OUTERMOST shell of an atom.

They are important because only these outer electrons take part in chemical bonding — they are the ones gained, lost or shared when atoms combine. The number of valence electrons determines an element's valency, the type of bond it forms (ionic or covalent), and therefore its chemical behaviour. Atoms with the same number of valence electrons behave chemically alike.

questions.question: In the ammonium ion (NH4+), all four N—H bonds are identical even though one is formed as a coordinate bond. Explain.
questions.answer:
Ammonia (NH₃) has three ordinary N—H covalent bonds (each formed by N and H sharing one electron each) and one LONE PAIR on nitrogen.

When NH₃ reacts with an H⁺ ion, nitrogen DONATES its lone pair to the H⁺, forming a fourth N—H bond — a COORDINATE bond (both electrons came from nitrogen).

Although this fourth bond is formed differently (by donation rather than mutual sharing), once it exists it consists of the SAME thing as the others: a shared pair of electrons between N and H. The electrons cannot be told apart, so all four N—H bonds have the same length, strength and energy. Hence in NH₄⁺ the four bonds are completely identical (equivalent), and the positive charge is spread over the whole ion.

questions.question: Why are noble gases such as helium, neon and argon chemically unreactive?
questions.answer:
Noble gases are unreactive because their OUTERMOST shells are completely filled — helium has 2 electrons (a full K shell) and neon, argon and the others have 8 electrons (a complete octet) in their outer shell.

A fully filled outer shell is the most stable, lowest-energy arrangement of electrons. Such atoms have no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons, so they do not form chemical bonds under ordinary conditions. This is exactly the stable configuration that all other atoms try to reach when they bond.

questions.question: Why is sodium chloride described as an electrovalent compound?
questions.answer:
Sodium chloride is called an ELECTROVALENT (ionic) compound because it is formed by the complete TRANSFER of electrons from one atom to another, producing charged ions.

Sodium (2, 8, 1) transfers its single valence electron to chlorine (2, 8, 7). This gives a Na⁺ cation and a Cl⁻ anion, each with a stable octet. The bond between them — the electrovalent bond — is the strong electrostatic attraction between these oppositely charged ions. Because the bond arises from electron transfer (producing 'electro' charges with 'valency'), it is called electrovalent.

questions.question: In which states do ionic compounds conduct electricity, and why?
questions.answer:
Ionic compounds conduct electricity in TWO states: when MOLTEN (melted) and when DISSOLVED in water (aqueous solution). They do NOT conduct in the solid state.

The reason is that conduction requires charge carriers that are free to move. In the solid, the ions are locked in fixed positions in the crystal lattice, so they cannot move and the solid does not conduct. When the compound is melted or dissolved, the lattice breaks up and the ions become free to move and carry the current.

questions.question: Explain the bonding in methane (CH4) and state how carbon and hydrogen complete their outer shells.
questions.answer:
Carbon (Z = 6, configuration 2, 4) has 4 valence electrons and needs 4 more to complete its octet. Each hydrogen atom has 1 electron and needs 1 more to reach the helium duet.

Carbon SHARES one electron pair with each of FOUR hydrogen atoms, forming four single C—H covalent bonds. Each shared pair has one electron from carbon and one from hydrogen.

Result: carbon now has 8 electrons in its outer shell (4 shared pairs) — a complete octet. Each hydrogen now has 2 electrons (one shared pair) — a complete duet. So methane consists of four equivalent single covalent bonds, and every atom has a stable outer shell.

questions.question: Why are most covalent compounds poor conductors of electricity?
questions.answer:
Most covalent compounds are poor conductors (non-electrolytes) because they are made of neutral MOLECULES and contain NO free ions or free electrons.

Electric current is carried by charged particles that are free to move. Since covalent compounds have no mobile charged particles — the electrons are all tied up in shared pairs within the molecules — there is nothing to carry the current. Hence they do not conduct electricity in the solid, liquid or dissolved state (a few exceptions, like acids in water, form ions and do conduct).

questions.question: Give three points of difference between ionic and covalent compounds.
questions.answer:
Three differences between ionic and covalent compounds:

1. STRUCTURE / PARTICLES: ionic compounds are made of ions held in a giant lattice, whereas covalent compounds are made of discrete molecules.

2. MELTING AND BOILING POINTS: ionic compounds have HIGH melting and boiling points (strong lattice forces); covalent compounds have LOW melting and boiling points (weak forces between molecules).

3. ELECTRICAL CONDUCTIVITY: ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water (free ions); covalent compounds generally do NOT conduct (no free ions or electrons).

(A fourth difference: ionic compounds dissolve in water/polar solvents, while covalent compounds usually dissolve in non-polar organic solvents.)

questions.question:
Common salt (sodium chloride) is the most familiar ionic compound. It is formed when sodium (Z = 11, configuration 2, 8, 1) reacts with chlorine (Z = 17, configuration 2, 8, 7). The reaction involves a transfer of electrons, after which the resulting particles arrange themselves in a regular pattern.
(a) Which atom loses an electron and which gains one?
(b) Write the electronic configurations of the two ions formed.
(c) Name the type of bond and the force holding the ions together.
(d) Why is the formula NaCl and not NaCl2?
questions.answer:
(a) SODIUM loses one electron (it has 1 extra electron over a stable octet); CHLORINE gains that electron (it is 1 short of an octet).
(b) Na⁺ has the configuration 2, 8 (like neon); Cl⁻ has the configuration 2, 8, 8 (like argon). Both now have stable octets.
(c) The bond is an IONIC (electrovalent) bond. The ions are held together by strong ELECTROSTATIC forces of attraction between the oppositely charged Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
(d) Sodium loses only ONE electron (forming Na⁺) and each chlorine gains only ONE electron (forming Cl⁻). One Na⁺ exactly balances one Cl⁻, so they combine in a 1 : 1 ratio — giving NaCl. NaCl₂ would require sodium to give up two electrons, which it cannot do (it has only one valence electron), and the charges would not balance.
questions.explanation: Apply electron transfer, ion configurations, electrostatic bonding and charge balance to NaCl.

questions.question:
A student tests two solids in the laboratory. Solid A melts at 801 °C, dissolves easily in water, and the solution conducts electricity. Solid B melts at 80 °C, does not dissolve in water, and neither the solid nor any melt of it conducts electricity.
(a) Classify A and B as ionic or covalent.
(b) Explain the melting-point difference.
(c) Explain why A's solution conducts but B does not.
(d) Predict whether B would dissolve in a non-polar solvent like petrol.
questions.answer:
(a) Solid A is an IONIC compound; Solid B is a COVALENT compound.
(b) A has a high melting point (801 °C) because its ions are held in a giant lattice by strong electrostatic forces that need a lot of energy to break. B has a low melting point (80 °C) because it consists of discrete molecules held by weak intermolecular forces, which are easily overcome.
(c) A's solution conducts because, when the ionic solid dissolves in water, the ions become free to move and carry the current. B has no ions at all — only neutral molecules — so neither the solid nor its melt nor any solution conducts.
(d) Yes — B is covalent and probably non-polar, so it is likely to dissolve in a non-polar solvent such as petrol (like dissolves like).
questions.explanation: Classify by properties; relate melting point, conductivity and solubility to bonding type.

questions.question:
Many gases in the air are simple covalent molecules. Hydrogen exists as H2, oxygen as O2 and nitrogen as N2. In each, the atoms share electrons so that each atom completes its outer shell.
(a) State the type of bond (single/double/triple) in each of H2, O2 and N2.
(b) How many electron pairs are shared in each?
(c) Which of these molecules has the strongest bond, and what consequence does this have?
(d) Why do these atoms share electrons rather than transfer them?
questions.answer:
(a) H₂ has a SINGLE bond; O₂ has a DOUBLE bond; N₂ has a TRIPLE bond.
(b) H₂ shares 1 pair; O₂ shares 2 pairs; N₂ shares 3 pairs of electrons.
(c) N₂ has the strongest bond (the triple bond N≡N). As a consequence, a large amount of energy is needed to break it, so nitrogen gas is rather unreactive (inert) under ordinary conditions.
(d) These are all non-metal atoms with similar (high) tendencies to attract electrons. Neither atom can pull an electron completely away from the other, so instead of transferring electrons (which would form ions), they SHARE electrons to complete their octets/duets — forming covalent bonds.
questions.explanation: Identify bond order, shared pairs, bond strength and why non-metals share.

questions.question:
Water is described as a polar molecule. In each O—H bond, the oxygen atom attracts the shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen does. This unequal sharing gives the molecule special properties, including its ability to dissolve many substances.
(a) What is meant by a polar covalent bond?
(b) Which atom in the O—H bond is δ− and which is δ+?
(c) Why is water able to dissolve ionic compounds like NaCl?
(d) Contrast this with the O=O bond in oxygen, which is non-polar.
questions.answer:
(a) A POLAR covalent bond is a covalent bond between two different atoms in which the shared electron pair is attracted more strongly by one atom (the more electronegative one), creating a small negative charge (δ−) on it and a small positive charge (δ+) on the other.
(b) In the O—H bond, OXYGEN is δ− (it pulls the electrons towards itself) and HYDROGEN is δ+.
(c) Because water molecules are polar, their δ− oxygen ends attract the positive cations and their δ+ hydrogen ends attract the negative anions of an ionic compound. The water molecules surround and pull the ions out of the lattice, so the ionic compound dissolves.
(d) In O₂ the two atoms are IDENTICAL, so they attract the shared electrons equally. There is no separation of charge, so the O=O bond (and the O₂ molecule) is NON-POLAR — unlike the polar O—H bonds in water.
questions.explanation: Define polar bond, identify δ charges, link polarity to dissolving ions, contrast with non-polar O2.

questions.question:
When ammonia gas (NH3) is passed into hydrochloric acid, the ammonium ion (NH4+) is formed. In ammonia, the nitrogen atom has three N—H bonds and one lone pair of electrons. The hydrogen ion (H+) has no electrons.
(a) What type of bond forms between the nitrogen lone pair and the H+ ion?
(b) Why can H+ not form an ordinary covalent bond with nitrogen here?
(c) How is this bond shown in a diagram?
(d) Why are all four N—H bonds in NH4+ identical afterwards?
questions.answer:
(a) A COORDINATE (dative) bond forms between the nitrogen lone pair and the H⁺ ion.
(b) An ordinary covalent bond needs EACH atom to contribute one electron to the shared pair. The H⁺ ion has NO electrons of its own to contribute, so it cannot form an ordinary covalent bond. Instead, nitrogen supplies BOTH electrons of the shared pair — a coordinate bond.
(c) A coordinate bond is shown by an ARROW (→) pointing from the donor (nitrogen) to the acceptor (the H⁺), i.e. N→H, distinguishing it from the plain lines of ordinary bonds.
(d) Although the fourth bond is formed differently, it ends up as a shared pair of electrons between N and H, exactly like the other three. The electrons are indistinguishable, so all four N—H bonds have the same length, strength and energy — they are identical, and the + charge is spread over the whole ion.
questions.explanation: Coordinate bond formation, donor/acceptor, arrow notation, and equivalence of bonds in NH4+.

questions.question:
Two compounds are studied. Compound P is a hard crystalline solid, melts at a very high temperature, conducts electricity when molten, and dissolves in water. Compound Q is a soft solid with a low melting point, does not conduct electricity in any state, and dissolves in kerosene but not in water.
(a) Identify the bond type in P and in Q.
(b) What kind of particles make up P and Q?
(c) Explain the conductivity difference.
(d) Explain the solubility difference.
questions.answer:
(a) Compound P contains IONIC (electrovalent) bonds; compound Q contains COVALENT bonds.
(b) P is made up of oppositely charged IONS arranged in a giant lattice. Q is made up of discrete neutral MOLECULES.
(c) P conducts when molten because its ions become free to move and carry current; Q never conducts because it has no free ions or electrons — only neutral molecules.
(d) P dissolves in water because water is polar and pulls the ions out of the lattice; it would not dissolve in kerosene (non-polar). Q dissolves in kerosene (a non-polar solvent) because Q is non-polar (like dissolves like) but does not dissolve in water. This contrast in solubility follows directly from their bond types.
questions.explanation: Distinguish ionic vs covalent by structure, conductivity and solubility (like dissolves like).

questions.question:
The noble gases helium (2), neon (2, 8) and argon (2, 8, 8) are found as single, unbonded atoms in air. Sodium (2, 8, 1), oxygen (2, 6) and chlorine (2, 8, 7) are never found as free single atoms — they always occur combined or as molecules.
(a) What is special about the electronic configuration of the noble gases?
(b) State the octet rule.
(c) How many electrons must sodium lose, and oxygen gain, to reach a noble-gas configuration?
(d) Why does this explain why noble gases do not bond but sodium and oxygen do?
questions.answer:
(a) The noble gases have completely filled OUTERMOST shells — 2 electrons for helium and 8 (an octet) for neon and argon. This is the most stable electron arrangement.
(b) The OCTET RULE: atoms combine by gaining, losing or sharing electrons so as to attain eight electrons in their outermost shell (a duet of 2 for the smallest atoms), like the nearest noble gas.
(c) Sodium (2, 8, 1) must LOSE 1 electron to reach the neon configuration (2, 8). Oxygen (2, 6) must GAIN 2 electrons to reach the neon configuration (2, 8).
(d) Noble gases already have a full, stable outer shell, so they have no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons — they do not bond. Sodium and oxygen have incomplete (unstable) outer shells, so they react and form bonds in order to reach the stable noble-gas configuration.
questions.explanation: Noble-gas stability and the octet rule explain bonding behaviour.

questions.question:
An element X has atomic number 12 and an element Y has atomic number 8. They combine to form a compound.
(a) Write the electronic configurations of X and Y.
(b) State the number of valence electrons and the valency of each.
(c) Will X lose or gain electrons? Will Y lose or gain electrons?
(d) Write the formula of the compound formed and name the type of bond.
questions.answer:
(a) X (Z = 12): 2, 8, 2. Y (Z = 8): 2, 6.
(b) X has 2 valence electrons → valency 2 (it is a metal, magnesium). Y has 6 valence electrons → valency = 8 − 6 = 2 (it is a non-metal, oxygen).
(c) X (2, 8, 2) will LOSE its 2 valence electrons to form X²⁺ (configuration 2, 8). Y (2, 6) will GAIN 2 electrons to form Y²⁻ (configuration 2, 8).
(d) X loses 2 electrons and Y gains 2, so they combine in a 1 : 1 ratio. The formula is XY (which is MgO, magnesium oxide). The bond is an IONIC (electrovalent) bond, formed by electron transfer.
questions.explanation: Configurations, valency, electron transfer and 1:1 formula for MgO.

questions.question:
Covalent compounds show a range of behaviour. Carbon dioxide and methane are gases, wax is a soft solid, and naphthalene (used in moth balls) sublimes easily. None of these conduct electricity, and most do not dissolve in water, though some, like sugar, do.
(a) Why do covalent compounds generally have low melting and boiling points?
(b) Why do most covalent compounds not conduct electricity?
(c) Why are many covalent compounds insoluble in water?
(d) Why does sugar, a covalent compound, dissolve in water?
questions.answer:
(a) Covalent compounds exist as discrete molecules held together by WEAK forces between the molecules. Only a little energy is needed to separate the molecules, so they melt and boil at low temperatures (many are gases or liquids).
(b) They contain no free ions or free electrons — all the electrons are tied up in shared pairs within neutral molecules. With no mobile charge carriers, they cannot conduct electricity.
(c) Many covalent compounds are non-polar. Water is polar, and 'like dissolves like': non-polar molecules are not attracted by polar water, so they do not dissolve in it (they dissolve in non-polar organic solvents instead).
(d) Sugar is a POLAR covalent compound — its molecules have polar groups that can attract and be attracted by polar water molecules. Because both are polar, sugar dissolves in water even though it is covalent.
questions.explanation: Low m.p./b.p., non-conduction, water-insolubility and the polar exception (sugar).

questions.question:
Ammonia (NH3) is an important covalent compound. In it, the nitrogen atom (2, 5) is bonded to three hydrogen atoms, and nitrogen is left with one lone pair of electrons.
(a) How many covalent bonds does nitrogen form in NH3, and of what type?
(b) How does nitrogen complete its octet?
(c) What is a lone pair?
(d) The lone pair lets ammonia do something special when it meets an H+ ion. What is it?
questions.answer:
(a) Nitrogen forms THREE single covalent bonds (three N—H bonds), one with each hydrogen atom.
(b) Nitrogen (2, 5) has 5 valence electrons. By sharing one electron pair with each of three hydrogens, it gains a share in 3 more electrons, giving it 8 outer electrons (3 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair) — a complete octet. Each hydrogen completes its duet of 2.
(c) A LONE PAIR is a pair of valence electrons on an atom that is NOT used in bonding — here, the pair left on nitrogen after forming the three N—H bonds.
(d) Using this lone pair, ammonia can form a COORDINATE (dative) bond with an H⁺ ion (which has no electrons). Nitrogen donates its lone pair to the H⁺, forming the ammonium ion NH₄⁺.
questions.explanation: NH3 bonding, octet completion, lone pair and coordinate-bond formation to give NH4+.
